title: Beer Color SRM Calculator Morey 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Calculate Your Beer's SRM Color with the Morey Formula
description: Calculate beer color SRM using the Morey formula. Input malt weight, Lovibond degrees, and batch volume to predict final color and match BJCP style ranges.
intro:
Every homebrewer and craft brewer has experienced the frustration of pulling a beer from the fermentor only to find it came out noticeably lighter or darker than the target style. Whether you're aiming for the bright golden clarity of a German Kölsch, the deep amber of an American Amber Ale, or the near-opaque blackness of a Russian Imperial Stout, nailing your beer's color starts at the recipe design stage — long before brew day.

**SRM (Standard Reference Method)** is the American standard for measuring beer color, expressed on a scale from 1 (ultra-pale straw, think light lagers) to 40+ (opaque black). It's measured spectrophotometrically at 430 nanometers using a 0.5 cm cell, but for recipe design purposes, you need a way to *predict* your SRM before you brew. That's where the **Morey equation** comes in.

Developed by Daniel Morey in 1993 and published in *Brewing Techniques*, the Morey formula uses a log-linear curve fit against thousands of real-world beers to predict final SRM from the grain bill. The key intermediate value is **MCU (Malt Color Units)**, calculated as (weight in lbs × Lovibond degrees) ÷ batch volume in gallons for each malt addition. Morey then transforms total MCU into SRM using the equation **SRM = 1.4922 × MCU^0.6859**, which handles both very pale and very dark beers more accurately than the older linear Mosher or Daniels methods. It's the algorithm behind BeerSmith, Brewer's Friend, and most professional recipe software.

This calculator lets you enter up to three malt categories — base malts, crystal/caramel malts, and roasted/chocolate malts — along with their Lovibond ratings and your final batch volume. The tool converts kg and liters to the lbs/gallons units the formula requires, sums the MCU contributions, and outputs your predicted SRM alongside the corresponding BJCP style color ranges so you can immediately see whether your recipe falls within target.

What makes this calculator uniquely useful is the transparency of the calculation: you see each malt's MCU contribution independently, so you can make targeted adjustments. Want to darken a pale ale by 2 SRM? The numbers tell you exactly how many grams of Crystal 60L to add. Brewing a Schwarzbier and worried your Carafa III is pushing you past style? You'll know before milling a single gram. Pair this tool with a water chemistry calculator and a gravity/efficiency estimator, and you have a complete recipe design workflow in one session.
keyTakeaway: **Morey: SRM = 1.4922 × MCU^0.6859**. Pale Ale 5-10 SRM, IPA 6-14, Stout 30-40+ SRM.

explanation:
## What is SRM

The **SRM (Standard Reference Method)** is the American beer color scale, measured at 430 nm. It runs from 1 (pale straw) to 40+ (black). In Europe, **EBC = SRM × 1.97**.

## Morey Formula

```
MCU = Σ(kg × °L × 2.205) / volume_gallons
SRM = 1.4922 × MCU^0.6859
```

It's non-linear: at higher MCU, marginal contribution decreases. That's why an extra 100g of chocolate in a stout doesn't shift the color much.

## SRM by Beer Style

| Style | SRM | Color |
|---|---|---|
| Light Lager | 2-4 | Pale straw |
| Witbier | 2-4 | Cloudy white |
| Hefeweizen | 3-9 | Yellow-amber |
| **Pale Ale** | 5-10 | Golden |
| **IPA** | 6-14 | Golden-copper |
| Amber Ale | 10-17 | Amber |
| Brown Ale | 18-35 | Brown |
| Porter | 22-40 | Dark brown |
| **Stout** | 30-40+ | Black |

## Typical Malt Lovibond Ratings

| Malt | °L |
|---|---|
| Pilsner | 1.5-2 |
| Pale 2-row | 2 |
| Munich | 8-10 |
| Vienna | 4 |
| Crystal 60 | 60 |
| Crystal 120 | 120 |
| Chocolate | 300-400 |
| Black Patent | 500 |
| Roasted Barley | 300-500 |

## Common Mistakes

1. **Ignoring the boil**: Maillard reactions add 1-2 SRM in long boils.
2. **Confusing Lovibond with EBC**: Different scales entirely.
3. **Using Mosher instead**: Overstates dark malts; Morey is more accurate.

See [ABV Calculator](/calculadora-abv-cerveza-og-fg) to complete your recipe.

faq.q: What does SRM stand for and how is it actually measured?
faq.a: SRM stands for Standard Reference Method, the American system for quantifying beer color developed by the American Society of Brewing Chemists (ASBC). In a laboratory setting, SRM is measured by shining light at 430 nanometers through a 0.5 cm column of beer and recording how much light is absorbed. The measurement is expressed as: SRM = 12.7 × D × A430, where D is the dilution factor and A430 is the absorbance reading. In practical brewing, however, SRM is almost always *predicted* from the grain bill using formulas like Morey's rather than measured post-brew. The SRM scale runs from 1 (pale straw — think Bud Light or a German Pilsner) up to 40+ for opaque black stouts and porters. Beyond roughly 40 SRM, the scale becomes less meaningful visually because the beer appears uniformly black regardless of additional color contribution.

faq.q: Why is the Morey formula preferred over Mosher or Daniels methods?
faq.a: There are three commonly cited SRM prediction methods: Mosher (linear: SRM = 0.3 × MCU + 4.7), Daniels (linear: SRM = 0.2 × MCU + 8.4), and Morey (log-linear: SRM = 1.4922 × MCU^0.6859). The Mosher and Daniels formulas are linear approximations that work reasonably well in the mid-range (roughly 5–20 SRM) but significantly overestimate color for very pale beers and underestimate it for very dark beers. Morey's formula, developed in 1993, was curve-fit against a large dataset of real commercial and homebrewed beers across the full color spectrum. The power function (MCU^0.6859) captures the non-linear relationship between grain bill color and final beer color far more accurately. This is why BeerSmith, Brewer's Friend, and most professional recipe software use the Morey formula as their default. If you're brewing anything outside the 5–15 SRM range, Morey is meaningfully more accurate.

faq.q: What are MCU (Malt Color Units) and how are they calculated?
faq.a: MCU stands for Malt Color Units, and it's the intermediate value the Morey formula uses before converting to SRM. For each malt in your grain bill, MCU is calculated as: MCU = (weight in lbs × Lovibond degrees) ÷ batch volume in US gallons. You calculate MCU for each malt separately, then sum them to get total MCU, which feeds into the Morey equation. For example, 8.8 lbs (4 kg) of 2°L base malt in a 5.28-gallon (20L) batch contributes MCU = (8.8 × 2) ÷ 5.28 = 3.33. A 0.66 lb (0.3 kg) addition of 60°L Crystal in the same batch contributes MCU = (0.66 × 60) ÷ 5.28 = 7.5. Total MCU = 10.83, which Morey converts to SRM = 1.4922 × 10.83^0.6859 ≈ 8.2 SRM. This calculator handles the kg-to-lbs and liter-to-gallon conversions automatically.

faq.q: How do I convert SRM to EBC, and which do European recipes use?
faq.a: SRM and EBC (European Brewery Convention) are both widely used color standards but with different scales. The conversion is: EBC = SRM × 1.97, or inversely SRM = EBC ÷ 1.97. Some practical reference points: A 5 SRM American Pale Ale is 9.9 EBC; a 14 SRM IPA is 27.6 EBC; a 35 SRM Stout is 69 EBC. European recipes, German brewing texts, and most commercial European ingredient specifications use EBC. British brewing literature often uses SRM (historically called °Lovibond at the macro scale, though technically different). If you're following a German Weissbier recipe that specifies 8 EBC, that's 4.1 SRM. This calculator outputs SRM, but the EBC equivalent is shown alongside for cross-reference. Note that EBC measures absorbance at 430nm in a 1 cm cell (vs. 0.5 cm for ASBC/SRM), which is the source of the 1.97 factor.

faq.q: Does boil time or boil intensity affect my beer's final color?
faq.a: Yes, significantly. The Morey formula predicts color contribution from your grain bill only — it does not account for Maillard browning reactions that occur during the boil. In practice, a vigorous 60-minute boil can add approximately 1–3 SRM above the Morey prediction. A 90-minute boil (common for Pilsners and light lagers to drive off DMS) can add 2–4 SRM. High-gravity wort concentrations and vigorous rolling boils amplify this effect. The browning occurs between reducing sugars and amino acids at high temperatures. Practical strategies to minimize unintended darkening: use a covered boil for the first 15 minutes, avoid scorching on the kettle bottom, use a hop spider to prevent hop debris from darkening, and consider reducing total boil time if your target is very pale (under 5 SRM). Conversely, if you want a deeper color without additional specialty malt, a longer boil is a legitimate technique — particularly in Scottish Ales where caramelization is a stylistic feature.

faq.q: What Lovibond values should I expect from common malts?
faq.a: Lovibond (°L) is the color rating assigned to individual malts, and knowing typical ranges helps you build recipes predictably. Base malts are light: Pilsner Malt 1.5–2°L, 2-Row Pale Malt 1.8–2.5°L, Munich Malt 6–10°L, Vienna Malt 3–5°L, Wheat Malt 1.5–3°L, Maris Otter 3–4°L. Crystal/caramel malts span a wide range: Crystal 10L, Crystal 20L, Crystal 40L, Crystal 60L, Crystal 80L, Crystal 120L (all at their respective °L values), Caramunich I/II/III (25–55°L), Special B (~180°L). Roasted malts are very dark: Biscuit/Victory (25–35°L), Brown Malt (65°L), Chocolate Malt (300–400°L), Black Patent Malt (500–525°L), Roasted Barley (300°L), Carafa Special I/II/III (300–525°L). Always check your specific malt supplier's spec sheet — there's meaningful variation between maltsters, and a 40°L crystal from one supplier may be 45°L from another.

faq.q: Why might my finished beer look darker or lighter than the Morey prediction?
faq.a: Several brewing variables can cause your actual beer color to deviate from the Morey prediction. Factors that *darken* beyond prediction: extended boil time (Maillard reactions), very high mash temperatures (above 158°F/70°C), low mash pH (below 5.2), scorching on the kettle bottom, high-gravity wort concentration, oxidation during transfer or packaging, and dark brewing water with high bicarbonate. Factors that *lighten* below prediction: very short boil times, cold-side fining agents (gelatin, isinglass) that drop haze, filtration that removes colored compounds, very light-colored adjuncts (rice, corn, sugar) diluting the grain bill color, and highly flocculent yeast that drops clear quickly. In practice, experienced brewers add 1–2 SRM to their Morey prediction for any beer with a 60+ minute vigorous boil, and may subtract SRM when using significant adjunct additions. The Morey formula is a strong starting prediction but should be calibrated over multiple batches with your specific setup.

faq.q: How do BJCP style guidelines use SRM ranges?
faq.a: The Beer Judge Certification Program (BJCP) Style Guidelines include minimum and maximum SRM values for every recognized beer style, and judges do evaluate color as part of the Appearance category (3 points out of 50 in the scoresheet). Key BJCP SRM ranges to know: American Light Lager 2–3, German Pilsner 2–5, Kölsch 3.5–5, American Blonde Ale 3–6, American Pale Ale 5–10, American Wheat 3–6, American Amber Ale 10–17, California Common 10–14, American IPA 6–14, American Porter 22–40, American Stout 30–40, Russian Imperial Stout 30–40, Schwarzbier 17–30, Doppelbock 6–25, Weissbier 2–8, Dunkelweizen 14–23, Märzen 8–17, Flanders Red Ale 10–17. For competition brewing, being significantly outside the listed SRM range will cost you Appearance points and may make judges skeptical before they even taste the beer. This calculator outputs the BJCP style range alongside your SRM prediction for quick reference.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for extract brewing, not just all-grain?
faq.a: Yes, with one important adjustment. For extract brewing, the Lovibond rating of your malt extract is the key input. Dry Malt Extract (DME) and Liquid Malt Extract (LME) come pre-rated in Lovibond: Pilsen LME is typically 2–3°L, Extra Light DME 3°L, Light LME/DME 3–5°L, Amber LME/DME 10–15°L, Dark LME/DME 20–30°L, Munich LME 8–10°L. Enter the extract weight (in kg) and its Lovibond rating as your 'base malt' input. If you're doing a partial mash (steeping specialty grains on top of extract), add those specialty malts in the crystal or roasted malt fields with their respective Lovibond ratings. The formula works identically regardless of whether color comes from grain or extract. Note that extracts are often somewhat darker than equivalent all-grain wort due to processing, so your actual beer may come out 1–3 SRM darker than the prediction when using LME specifically.

faq.q: What is the difference between Lovibond degrees and SRM at the malt level?
faq.a: At the malt level, Lovibond (°L) and SRM are often used interchangeably in homebrew contexts, but they are technically different measurement methods. °Lovibond (developed by Joseph Lovibond in the 1880s) is a visual color comparison method where a sample is matched against a set of colored glass slides. The ASBC SRM (spectrophotometric measurement at 430nm) replaced it as the analytical standard in commercial brewing. For malts, the two scales are approximately equivalent in the low-to-mid range (under about 50°L), so a Crystal 60L malt is close to Crystal 60 SRM as a malt color descriptor. However, above 50–80°L, the scales diverge meaningfully. In practice, most malt spec sheets list °Lovibond for light-to-medium specialty malts and may switch to SRM or EBC for very dark malts. For this calculator, use whatever value appears on your malt's specification sheet (°L, SRM, or convert from EBC by dividing by 1.97) — the difference in the low range is negligible for recipe design purposes.

faq.q: How do adjuncts like oats, wheat, corn, or sugar affect SRM?
faq.a: Unmalted or minimally processed adjuncts generally contribute very little color. Flaked Oats: 1–2°L, essentially color-neutral, used in New England IPAs and Oatmeal Stouts. Flaked Wheat: 1–2°L, similarly neutral. Flaked Corn (Maize): 0.5–1°L, used in American Lagers to lighten color. Rice: ~0.5°L, even lighter than corn. Table Sugar (sucrose) or Corn Sugar (dextrose): 0°L, contributes zero color. Lactose: ~1°L. Honey: 1–3°L depending on type. Molasses: can add significant color, treat as a dark specialty ingredient. In this calculator, you can add adjuncts to the base malt field with their Lovibond rating if they're a meaningful portion of the grain bill. However, because most adjuncts are very light, they primarily affect SRM by *diluting* the colored malt contributions rather than adding their own color — a 20% oat addition in an NEIPA slightly lightens the final color versus an all-malt base.

faq.q: Is the Morey formula accurate enough for commercial or professional brewing?
faq.a: The Morey formula is an excellent *predictive* tool but has inherent limitations at the commercial scale. It was curve-fit against a dataset of predominantly homebrewed and small-craft beers, and while it performs well across the full color spectrum, commercial breweries typically verify color spectrophotometrically on every batch using ASBC or EBC methods. For professional quality control, the Morey prediction is used at the recipe design stage, but actual SRM measurement post-brew is standard practice. Factors that increase prediction error at commercial scale: very large grain bills where mash efficiency fluctuates, blending of multiple wort streams, long boil times or evaporation rates above 10%, and filtration or centrifugation that removes colored particles. For homebrewing and craft production up to roughly 10-barrel batches, Morey predictions are typically accurate within ±1–3 SRM, which is sufficient for most style compliance purposes. Professional brewers who need tighter tolerances (e.g., contract brewing to a client's color spec) should calibrate the Morey output against measured SRM from previous batches and apply a correction factor specific to their system.
